newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Six countries cited for violating workers' rights.
newsitem.headline: Six countries cited for violating workers' rights.

text.p: An international labour committee accused Burma, Iran, Morocco, Nigeria, Sudan and Swaziland on Thursday of violating fundamental standards. The complaints included the use of forced labour, discrimination and denial of workers' right to organise.

The nearly 400 delegates to the International Labour Conference who took part in the annual forum's committee on the application of standards, singled out Burma, Nigeria and Sudan for "continued failure to implement ratified Conventions".
"It is a political sanction," an official of the International Labour Organisation (ILO) told Reuters.
The United Nations agency hosts the talks which bring together some 2,000 delegates from its 174 member states.

"In its report to the 1997 International Labour Conference, the committee on the application of standards determined that the non-application by Iran, Myanmar (Burma), Morocco, Nigeria, Sudan and Swaziland of fundamental international labour standards, including forced labour, discrimination and denial of the right to organise, were a cause of special concern," ILO said in a statement on the last day of the three-week meeting.
The tripartite committee, composed of delegates from governments, employers' and workers' groups, heard 27 cases.
Sudan was cited for long-standing accusations of forced and slave labour, and was urged to fully apply a 1930 convention.

"The accusations against Sudan involve trading in slaves and the imposition of slavery, servitude and forced labour on people from the Dinka, Shilluk and Nuer tribes and the tribes of the Nuba mountains in southern Sudan," the ILO statement said.
Sudan responded that the charges were politically-motivated, saying areas where forced labour allegedly took place were held by rebels or marked by tribal warfare, according to the ILO.

Burma was cited for continued failure to implement a convention guaranteeing freedom of association and the right to organise. The committee expressed great concern with the "total absence of progress" and urged legislative and other changes.
Nigeria was accused of violating the same 1948 convention. The committee called on Lagos to look into the situation of imprisoned union leaders.
Iran was accused of systematically violating a convention on discrimination in employment by discriminating against women and against religions not officially recognised such as the Baha'is.
Morocco was cited for complaints concerning anti-union discrimination and interference in trade union activities, while Swaziland was cited for violating the freedom of association.
